questions.subject: Ibibio
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose an incorrect explanation of the closure for /k/.
questions.prompt: A student writing an Ibibio pronunciation guide says that /k/ is made by closing both lips before releasing the air. Identify the consonant this instruction would describe instead and rewrite the instruction for /k/.
questions.answer: The instruction describes /p/. For /k/, raise the back of the tongue to the soft palate, block the airflow briefly, then release the closure.
questions.explanation: Both sounds involve a temporary closure and release. The articulators differ. The lips make the closure for /p/ and the back of the tongue and soft palate make it for /k/.

markingGuide.description: Name the back of the tongue and soft palate for /k/.
Describe a brief closure followed by release.

questions.subject: Ibibio
questions.learningObjective: Read written high and low tone marks in an Ibibio word.
questions.prompt: A learner transcribes the tone pattern of Èkámbá as high–high–high and the pattern of Údómó as high–high–high. Which entry needs a correction? Write the corrected pattern and identify the mark that supports the change.
questions.answer: Èkámbá needs correction. Its pattern is low–high–high. The grave accent on È marks low tone.
questions.explanation: The grave accent on the first vowel of Èkámbá marks a low tone, while the acute accents mark high tones. Údómó has three acute accents.

markingGuide.description: Identify the grave accent on È as evidence.

questions.subject: Ibibio
questions.learningObjective: Use an attested Ibibio loanword to explain adaptation of a borrowed form.
questions.prompt: In an Ibibio school glossary, a pupil pairs the English subject name “chemistry” with Kemistri. Another pupil argues that a borrowed word must have exactly the same spelling as its source. Use this pair to explain why the rule is wrong and point out one spelling change.
questions.answer: Kemistri is an Ibibio borrowing from English chemistry. Borrowed vocabulary can be adapted to the receiving language. For example, the initial English ch is written k in Kemistri.
questions.explanation: In this pair the name of the school subject is retained while the spelling is adapted. The pair supplies concrete evidence that borrowing does not require copying every letter.

markingGuide.description: Identify Kemistri as the Ibibio borrowing.
Explain that the receiving language may adapt the form.
Give an accurate spelling comparison, such as initial ch becoming k.
